rows.rule:
1. **Import:** customs value £10,000 already includes £400 freight. Separately chargeable excise £1,000 and packing £200 are not included. Taxable amount = £10,000 + £1,000 + £200 = **£11,200**. At an established 15% rate, tax = **£1,680**. Adding the £400 again would overstate tax by £60.
2. **Local production:** established comparable open-market value £8,000; production cost £6,000. At an established 15% rate, tax = **£1,200**, not £900. If disposal rights transfer before dispatch, leaving occurs on that transfer under paragraph 1(2)(b).
3. **No comparable supply:** no purchase price is available and evidenced cost price is £6,000. That establishes a floor of £6,000, not proof that any lower invoice price is acceptable. At 15%, tax on the floor is £900; confirm the final taxable valuation before using that amount.

rows.rule:
1. Establish eligible transaction tax **paid** in the supported period.
2. Calculate the import duty that would previously have applied in that same period. For imports subject to multiple historical rates, rule 4(2) requires a weighted average using broad goods categories and their proportions of total imports. Retain the categories, allocation basis, historical rates, customs declarations and purchase records. The Commissioner must be satisfied with the calculation and can require more evidence or withhold/adjust it.
3. Calculate the positive difference between transaction tax and counterfactual duty. If transaction tax is not higher, no deduction arises under rule 4(1).
4. Limit that amount to **50% of tax paid in the immediately preceding accounting period or year of assessment**. Use evidence of payment, not merely the assessed liability.
5. Apply eligibility, aid and other-support restrictions below. Deduct the permitted amount in computing assessable profits for the accounting period/year commencing on or after the Implementation Date; do not automatically put it into the period containing an import date. The announcement describes the first such period.

rows.rule: **Mixed-import illustration:** assume an evidenced £100,000 historical duty base, with accepted value proportions of 60% at a historical 10% rate and 40% at 0%. The weighted rate is 60% × 10% + 40% × 0% = **6%**, giving counterfactual duty of **£6,000**. Eligible transaction tax actually paid is £15,000, so the difference is £9,000. If immediately preceding-period tax paid was £12,000, the cap is £6,000 and the provisional deduction is **min(£9,000, £6,000) = £6,000**, subject to all remaining conditions. Assuming sufficient taxable profits and an independently established 15% income-tax rate, the resulting tax reduction would be **£900**, not £6,000. The example does not establish any real commodity's historical rate, valuation or allocation basis.

rows.rule: For Union goods, establish free-circulation status at the designated customs post before choosing Annex 19. A mixed Union/non-Union operation follows the separate Annex 21 route described by Customs; an Annex 19 authorisation alone does not establish that route. Regulation 3 of LN 2026/211 defines Union goods and indirect tax; regulation 4 applies the listed Union rules with the domestic replacements in Schedule 2. [LN 2026/211, regulations 3–4 and Schedules 1–2](https://www.gibraltarlaws.gov.gi/legislations/tgeu-implementation-special-customs-procedures-concerning-union-goods-regulations-2026-8575/download); [Annex 19 guidance, introduction](https://www.gibraltar.gov.gi/uploads/_PressOffice/Treaty%20Customs%20Guidance/Annex%2019%20Special%20Customs%20Procedures%20GN%20FINAL.pdf).

rows.rule: For Union-goods special procedures, first follow the OFT trading-licence process. After its formalities and before the licence is granted, apply to HM Customs Gibraltar for the procedure authorisation; OFT issues the licence after that authorisation. Warehousing/inward-processing preparation includes a premises plan and relevant segregation, traceable digital inventory, security, Customs access and a guarantee covering tax/duty. Temporary admission requires unaltered goods and a guarantee. Existing operators continuing after the transition keep the existing licence under the specific guidance exception, but still need the new procedure authorisation. These are published requirements, not approval of any actual premises or guarantee. [Guidance, sections 2–3 and 5.3–5.4](https://www.gibraltar.gov.gi/uploads/_PressOffice/Treaty%20Customs%20Guidance/Annex%2019%20Special%20Customs%20Procedures%20GN%20FINAL.pdf).

rows.rule: For authorised Union-goods warehousing, the T2GI ends when the Gibraltar IM7 clears; move the goods to the approved warehouse. Discharge through IM4 home use or the appropriate EX3 re-export, IM5 “5001” inward processing or IM9 destruction route. Warehousing permits storage and the specified usual handling such as packing, cleaning or refrigeration; further processing needs inward processing. Regulation 4(3) says the non-ship-supplies period is “between one month and nine months”; guidance 1.1.4 says it must exceed one month and be less than nine months. Do not decide an exact one- or nine-month boundary from the guidance alone. Ship supplies have no minimum. [LN 2026/188, regulation 4(3)](https://www.gibraltarlaws.gov.gi/legislations/tgeu-implementation-annex-19-regulations-2026-8553/download); [guidance 1.1](https://www.gibraltar.gov.gi/uploads/_PressOffice/Treaty%20Customs%20Guidance/Annex%2019%20Special%20Customs%20Procedures%20GN%20FINAL.pdf).

rows.rule: For Union-goods inward processing, close the T2GI using IM5 extended code “5001”, use the approved premises, and discharge both processed products and waste through the proper IM4, EX3, IM7 or IM9 route. Goods can instead be released for home use or re-exported unchanged. Temporary admission uses IM5, the declared use and an EX3 to close on re-export. Both have an ordinary three-month limit. A longer initial period or extension requires duly justified circumstances accepted by the designated post which opened the T2GI under regulation 4(6); an operator cannot grant its own extension. [Guidance 1.2–1.3](https://www.gibraltar.gov.gi/uploads/_PressOffice/Treaty%20Customs%20Guidance/Annex%2019%20Special%20Customs%20Procedures%20GN%20FINAL.pdf); [LN 2026/188, regulation 4(3), (6)](https://www.gibraltarlaws.gov.gi/legislations/tgeu-implementation-annex-19-regulations-2026-8553/download).

rows.rule: Keep the authorisation, arrival/clearance, inventory movements, removal declaration, tax/excise payments and discharge evidence together. Customs must send arrival advice on the presentation day and control results within three working days; a special-procedure message replaces proof of tax at that stage. Customs supplies case-by-case exit/destruction evidence or monthly tax proof for market releases. These are authority-to-authority reporting duties, not an extra three-day filing allowance for a trader. Missing proofs or failure to discharge can trigger the transfer of Member State VAT/excise under regulation 4(7). [LN 2026/188, regulation 4(2)–(7)](https://www.gibraltarlaws.gov.gi/legislations/tgeu-implementation-annex-19-regulations-2026-8553/download); [guidance section 4](https://www.gibraltar.gov.gi/uploads/_PressOffice/Treaty%20Customs%20Guidance/Annex%2019%20Special%20Customs%20Procedures%20GN%20FINAL.pdf).

rows.rule: The retained Imports and Exports Act requires an import entry within the relevant period, subject to sections 24 and 26: section 17 states seven clear days for air and fourteen clear days otherwise, using its defined report/arrival date and infectious-disease restriction proviso. Section 23 permits transit-shed deposit or sale of perishable goods on the specified failures, including the separate 21-clear-day clearance limb. These are residual entry rules. Section 2A and TGEU Schedule 1 paragraphs 12–14 make the Act subordinate to the treaty and disapply the old import-duty charge. They do not override immediate presentation, special transit or payment-before-release requirements. [Imports and Exports Act, sections 2A, 17, 21–23](https://www.gibraltarlaws.gov.gi/legislations/imports-and-exports-act-1986-423/download); [TGEU Act, Schedule 1 paragraphs 12–14](https://www.gibraltarlaws.gov.gi/uploads/legislations/treaty-on-gibraltar/2026-11/2026-11(15-07-26).pdf); [Transit guidance section 2](https://www.gibraltar.gov.gi/uploads/_PressOffice/Treaty%20Customs%20Guidance/Transit%20GN.pdf).

rows.rule: Within the Union-goods special-procedure regime, Schedule 2 Part A replacements for UCC Articles 102 and 108 require the notified debt to be paid within the Customs-prescribed period, no longer than ten days after notification, subject to the listed suspension cases. Release itself counts as notification where the declared amount equals the payable amount; a guaranteed aggregate notification period cannot exceed 30 days. Deferment under replacements 110–111 needs an application and Customs authorisation, with a guarantee if required, for at most 30 days beginning the day after notification. Other payment facilities under replacement 112 require a guarantee. This bounded regime does not confer a general ten- or thirty-day grace period on an ordinary IM4 release. [LN 2026/211, Schedule 2 Part A paragraphs 31, 37–41](https://www.gibraltarlaws.gov.gi/legislations/tgeu-implementation-special-customs-procedures-concerning-union-goods-regulations-2026-8575/download).

rows.rule: For a debt within that Union-goods special-procedure regime, identify the repayment/remission ground first: overcharge, defective/non-contract goods, Customs error or equity, or invalidated declaration. Replacement 116 normally uses a £10 threshold but permits a requested lower repayment. Replacement 121 gives three years from notification for its overcharge/error/equity limb, one year for defective/non-contract goods, and the applicable invalidation period for invalidated declarations. Evidence of unforeseeable circumstances or force majeure extends the first two periods; an Article 44 appeal suspends their running while it is pending. The applicant submits to HM Customs Gibraltar. These are not a verified deadline or form for the separate section 102 commercial-export refund. rows.rule: Failure to make a required entry under section 21 is punishable on summary conviction by a level 3 standard-scale fine. Section 109 covers materially untrue import/export documents or statements for goods whether dutiable or not; its knowing/reckless offence carries up to six months and a level 4 fine on summary conviction, or two years and twice level 5 on indictment. Section 117 supplies a level 4 summary fine where the Act gives no specific penalty. These are the retained customs offences subject to treaty primacy, not a newly verified universal transaction-tax penalty or a conversion of scale levels to pounds. rows.rule: Apply the single-undertaking test across direct and indirect majority voting, board appointment/removal, contractual/constitutional dominant influence and voting agreements under Article 2(2); separate company names do not reset the ceiling. Article 3(8)–(9) accounts for mergers, acquisitions and splits. Article 1 excludes the stated primary agricultural/fishery activities, certain processing/marketing cases, export-linked and domestic-preference aid; separated accounts/activities are required for its mixed-activity exception. Article 5 controls cumulation with other aid, including the same-cost intensity/amount limit. Do not apply EUR 300,000 mechanically to excluded sectors or substitute the separate services-of-general-economic-interest regime. rows.rule: Before relying on the transitional deduction, obtain the Commissioner’s acceptance of eligibility, the gross grant equivalent, linked-enterprise aid history and permissible remaining headroom. quotes: INTRODUCTION Special customs procedures are typically used when businesses need to store, move, process, repair or temporarily use goods without paying duties and taxes. The goods remain under customs control whilst they are subject to the special customs procedure. In many cases, the goods are

not released for free circulation in the customs territory during the procedure, and they may ultimately be re-exported rather than released for free circulation. Examples of special customs procedures under current Gibraltar legislation involve the use of “transit sheds” or “bonded warehouses”. Annex 19 of

the treaty provides for three special customs procedures: - Customs Warehousing; - Inward Processing; and - Temporary Admission. Customs Warehousing allows goods to be stored under customs supervision in Gibraltar without the immediate payment of transaction tax or excise duties (if applicable). Its objective is

to provide businesses with flexibility by suspending customs charges until the goods are either released for free circulation in Gibraltar or re- exported. It is typically used for inventory management, deferred import decisions, and situations where goods may ultimately be re-exported rather than sold in

the Gibraltar market. Inward Processing allows goods to be brought into Gibraltar for processing, manufacturing, assembly, repair, or maintenance without the immediate payment of transaction tax or excise duties (if applicable). Its objective is to support economic activity and international trade by suspending customs charges

while goods are being worked on, particularly where the resulting products may subsequently be re-exported. In the shipping industry, it is commonly used for the repair, refurbishment, or conversion of vessels and marine equipment, such as when a vessel enters Gibraltar for maintenance, or when

engines, navigation systems, spare parts, or other components are imported into Gibraltar for installation on ships before the vessel returns to international service. In motor vehicle industries, the procedure allows companies to import vehicles, or vehicle parts or components from outside the customs territory, modify,

assemble, or install them in vehicles, and then re- export the finished products without paying import duties or taxes on the imported items. Temporary Admission allows goods to enter Gibraltar without transaction tax having to be paid provided they are intended for re-export without undergoing

any substantial change except normal depreciation or necessary use. Its objective is to facilitate the temporary use of goods within Gibraltar while ensuring they remain under customs supervision and are not released for free circulation. It is typically used for situations where goods are brought

in for a limited period, such as professional equipment, exhibition goods or testing items before being re-exported in the same state. Subject to initial, time-limited transitional arrangements (see Point 5 below), the introduction of these regimes, in accordance with the treaty, will bring about important

changes which operators who have operated special customs procedures under current Gibraltar legislation should be aware of. This Guidance Note deals with the procedures for Union goods (Annex 19). A separate Guidance Note will deal with the procedures for non-Union goods (Annex 21). Please note

that if it is your intention to place both EU and non-EU goods under the procedures listed above, you must follow the procedure in the separate Guidance Note on Annex 21. Management of the procedure by HM Customs Gibraltar and the concept of special customs

procedure for “tax purposes”. The operation of Annex 19 special customs procedures will be authorised, managed and supervised by HM Customs Gibraltar applying Gibraltar legislation. Such legislation will be aligned with that applicable in the EU under the Union Customs Code. You will only need

to interact with HM Customs Gibraltar for the purposes of operating Annex 19 special customs procedures. Notably, the fact that the goods are to be placed in an Annex 19 special customs procedure does not need to be declared to the EU customs authorities at

the EU designated customs post. It is only upon the goods arriving in Gibraltar that it will need to be declared to HM Customs Gibraltar that the goods will be placed into an Annex 19 special customs procedure. The effect of doing so is to

suspend the levying of Gibraltar transaction tax and excise duties (where applicable) on those goods. This is why these Annex 19 special customs procedures are described as special customs procedures for Transaction Tax purposes. In other words, they are described in this manner because it

is only in relation to the suspension of the levying of Gibraltar transaction tax and excise duties that such goods are treated differently, from a tax perspective, as compared to goods which are released for free circulation in Gibraltar.

quotes: 1. IMPORTING THE GOODS TO BE PLACED IN AN ANNEX 19 SPECIAL CUSTOMS PROCEDURE. 1.1. Customs Warehousing. 1.1.1. Union goods destined for a customs warehouse would have undergone customs formalities at the Designated Customs Post (DCP) in Spain. 1.1.2. The consignment will then travel to

Gibraltar on a T2GI which will be closed upon clearance of HM Customs Gibraltar’s warehousing declaration (IM7) in Gibraltar. 1.1.3. Following clearance, the goods must be transported to an approved warehouse in Gibraltar where they will remain in suspense until they are removed via: (a)

import for free circulation (IM4); or (b) placement onto another Customs Procedure e.g. Re-exportation (EX3), Inward Processing (IM5 ‘5001’) or destruction (IM9). 1.1.4. Goods entered into an Annex 19 customs warehousing procedure can remain in that procedure for a period which needs to exceed 1

month but which is less than 9 months. In the case of ship supplies, the 1-month minimum period does not apply. 1.1.5. It is important to note that the customs warehousing procedure covers only the storage of the goods and processes known as Usual Forms

of Handling (UFH) which are limited to the following activities: (a) Preparing the goods for distribution or sale e.g. packing, wrapping etc; (b) Improving the appearance and/or marketability of the goods e.g. cleaning the goods; (c) Processing intended to preserve the goods e.g. refrigeration. 1.1.6.

Should you wish to undertake any other form of processing beyond the examples provided above, you will need to do so under the inward processing regime as detailed below. 1.2. Inward Processing. 1.2.1. Union goods destined for an inward processing procedure would have undergone EU

customs formalities at the Designated Customs Post (DCP) in Spain. 1.2.2. The consignment will then travel to Gibraltar on a T2GI which will be closed upon clearance of HM Customs Gibraltar’s inward processing declaration (IM5 with extended code ‘5001’) in Gibraltar. 1.2.3. Following clearance, goods

must be transported to the premises approved for inward processing. 1.2.4. The final product of the processing and any waste produced must then be removed from the procedure via: (a) Import for free circulation (IM4); or (b) Placement onto another customs procedure e.g. Re-exportation (EX3),

Warehousing (IM7) or destruction (IM9). 1.2.5. Goods can remain in an Annex 19 inward processing procedure for a maximum of 3 months. However, if there are duly justified circumstances, such procedures can be authorised, at the outset, for a period longer than 3 months or

extended for a period beyond the initial 3-month period authorised. 1.2.6. Goods placed under an Annex 19 inward processing procedure do not necessarily need to be processed i.e. the trader can instead choose to import the goods for home use or re-export the goods from

the inward processing procedure in the same state in which they were imported. 1.3. Temporary Admission. 1.3.1. Union goods destined for a temporary admission procedure would have undergone EU customs formalities at the Designated Customs Post (DCP) in Spain. 1.3.2. The consignment will then travel

to Gibraltar on a T2GI which will be closed upon clearance of HM Customs Gibraltar’s temporary admission declaration (IM5) in Gibraltar. 1.3.3. Following clearance by HM Customs Gibraltar, the goods can be used in Gibraltar for the purpose declared. 1.3.4. Once the goods are ready

to be exported out of Gibraltar, you must submit a re-export declaration (EX3) to cover the movement and close the procedure. 1.3.5. Goods can remain in an Annex 19 temporary admission procedure for a maximum of 3 months. However, if there are duly justified circumstances,
such procedures can be authorised, at the outset, for a period longer than 3 months or extended for a period beyond the initial 3-month period authorised.

quotes: Article 7 Transitional provisions 1. This Regulation shall apply to aid granted before its entry into force if the aid fulfils all the conditions laid down in this Regulation. 2. Any individual de minimis aid that was granted between 1 January 2014 and 31 December

2023 and that fulfils the conditions set out in Regulation (EU) No 1407/2013 shall be deemed not to meet all the criteria in Article 107(1) of the Treaty and shall therefore be exempt from the notification requirement in Article 108(3) of the Treaty. 3. At

the end of the period of validity of this Regulation, any de minimis aid which fulfils the conditions of this Regulation may be validly granted for a further period of 6 months. 4. Until the central register is set up and covers a period of

3 years, where a Member State intends to grant de minimis aid to an undertaking in accordance with this Regulation, that Member State shall inform the undertaking in written or electronic form of the amount of the aid expressed as a gross grant equivalent and

its de minimis character, referring directly to this Regulation. Where de minimis aid is granted to different undertakings in accordance with this Regulation on the basis of a scheme and different amounts of individual aid are granted to those undertakings under that scheme, the Member

State concerned may choose to fulfil its obligation by informing the undertakings of an amount corresponding to the maximum aid amount to be granted under that scheme. In such cases, the fixed sum shall be used for determining whether the ceiling laid down in Article

3(2) of this Regulation is complied with. Before granting the aid, the Member State shall obtain a declaration from the undertaking concerned, in written or electronic form, about any other de minimis aid received to which this Regulation or other de minimis regulations apply over
any period of 3 years.
